reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>肥胖症基层诊疗指南（2019年）</title><summary>本文是肥胖症基层诊疗指南（2019年），包括概述（定义、分类、流行病学）、病因和发病机制、诊断、鉴别诊断与转诊等内容。概述中指出肥胖症是机体脂肪总含量过多和/或局部含量增多及分布异常的慢性代谢性疾病，分为单纯性和继发性两大类，近30年患病率明显增长，成为全球重大公共卫生危机，我国肥胖形势严峻。病因和发病机制涉及能量代谢平衡失调、遗传、环境等因素。诊断包括临床表现、病史询问和诊断标准，诊断标准有以体重指数（bmi）诊断肥胖、以腰围诊断中心型肥胖等。鉴别诊断需结合病史、体征及实验室检查排除继发性肥胖症，还介绍了皮质醇增多症、甲状腺功能减退症、下丘脑或垂体疾病、胰岛相关疾病等的鉴别要点。</summary><hostname>掌桥科研</hostname><publisher>中华全科医师杂志2020年2月第19卷第2期</publisher><author_list><author name="中华医学会 中华医学会杂志社 中华医学会全科医学分会 中华医学会中华全科医师杂志编辑委员会 内分泌系统疾病基层诊疗指南编写专家组" /></author_list><url>https://m.zhangqiaokeyan.com/academic-journal-cn_chinese-journal-general-practitioners_thesis/0201278392272.html</url><publish_time>2020年2月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>平衡膳食指导对超重或肥胖高血压患者的干预效果</title><summary>摘要：目的 探讨平衡膳食指导对超重或肥胖高血压患者的干预效果。方法 回顾性分析2020年1月至2022年8月到北京市房山区良乡医院就诊的150例超重或肥胖高血压患者的临床资料，按营养干预方式分为对照组和观察组，每组75例。对照组采用常规营养健康教育，观察组在对照组基础上每天做饮食记录，每周规律随诊，由营养师给患者做膳食评价和平衡膳食指导。比较4周后两组膳食结构、人体成分和血压的变化情况。结果 通过营养健康教育和平衡膳食指导，在达到推荐的平衡膳食结构和总能量日常饮食方面，观察组患者食物达标比例均高于对照组（谷薯类80.00% vs. 48.00%、蔬菜类53.33% vs. 26.67%、水果类85.33% vs. 65.33%、肉蛋类88.00% vs. 66.67%、豆乳类66.67% vs. 41.33%、油脂类69.33% vs. 28.00%、盐68.00% vs. 26.67%和总能量93.33% vs. 52.00%），差异有统计学意义（P<0.05）；在达到宏量营养素合理比例方面，观察组患者食物达标比例均高于对照组（碳水化合物80.00% vs. 49.33%、脂肪74.67% vs. 32.00%和蛋白质92.00% vs. 74.67%），差异有统计学意义（P<0.05）。干预后观察组血压、体质量指数（body mass index，BMI）、腰臀比、体脂百分比、内脏脂肪面积均低于对照组，差异有统计学意义（P<0.05）。结论 平衡膳食指导对超重或肥胖高血压患者降低血压的效果显著。</summary><hostname>掌桥科研</hostname><publisher>慢性病学杂志</publisher><author_list><author name="王岩" affiliation="北京市房山区良乡医院（首都医科大学良乡教学医院）临床营养科" /></author_list><url>https://m.zhangqiaokeyan.com/academic-journal-cn_detail_thesis/02012103999491.html</url><publish_time>2023年4月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:3"><title>中国成人超重和肥胖症预防与控制指南（节录）</title><summary>(编者按:肥胖症是一种由多因素引起的慢性代谢性疾病,早在1948年世界卫生组织已将它列入疾病名单,并认为是ⅱ型糖尿病、心血管病、高血压、中风和多种癌症的危险因素。超重和肥胖症在一些发达国家和地区人群中的患病情况已呈流行趋势,我国目前体重超重者已达22.4%,肥胖者为3.01%,因此预防和控制肥胖症已成为刻不容缓的任务。国际生命科学学会中国办事处组织由多学科专家组成的“中国肥胖问题工作组”,对我国21个省、市、地区人群体重指数(bm)、腰围、血压、血糖、血脂等24万人的相关数据进行汇总分析,并据此提出“以bm值24为中国成人超重的界限,bm 28为肥胖的界限;男性腰围≥85 cm,女性腰围≥80 cm为腹部脂肪蓄积的界限”。工作组又编写了《中国成人超重和肥胖症预防与控制指南(试用)》,卫生部疾病控制司于2003年3月正式公布。现将与营养有关的内容节录如下,供参考。文中能量单位kcal 应用kJ 换算,1 kcal =4.18 kJ,请注意。</summary><publisher>营养学报</publisher><url>http://csjfyy.com/articles/E/070/030/020.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:4"><title>成人肥胖食养指南</title><summary>肥胖是一种慢性代谢性疾病,近些年来,全球超重和肥胖率正快速增长,已成为威胁人类健康的严重问题。根据《中国居民营养与慢性病状况报告(2020年)》显示,我国18岁及以上居民超重率、肥胖率分别为34.3%、16.4%,其中18~44岁、45~59岁和60岁及以上居民肥胖率分别为16.4%、18.3%和13.6%,我国居民肥胖率呈上升趋势。肥胖不但导致较高的过早死亡风险,还与各种慢性非传染性疾病的发生相关,包括2型糖尿病、脑卒中、冠心病、高血压、呼吸系统疾病、骨关节炎和胆结石等。肥胖甚至还与多种肿瘤的发生相关。2019年全国11.98%的心血管疾病死亡归因于高体质指数,死亡人数为54.95万。肥胖的流行以其高昂的医疗费用为国民经济带来了沉重的负担。有研究预测,到2030年我国成年人超重肥胖率可达65.3%,归因于超重肥胖的医疗费用可能为4180亿元人民币,约占全国医疗费用总额的21.5%,未来中国城乡居民超重肥胖率及其所造成的经济负担将呈上升趋势。因此,肥胖防控已刻不容缓。肥胖的发生虽然受遗传、环境和社会文化等因素共同影响,但根本原因是机体的能量摄入大于能量消耗,从而导致多余的能量以脂肪的形式在体内贮存。膳食营养和身体活动是肥胖防治的两大重要影响因素。减肥关键三分靠动,七分靠吃。以“辨证施膳”为核心的中医食养是在中医辨证施治指导下的非药物调养方法,强调根据体质、病因、病机、证候,给予不同食养方案,具有调和气血、平衡人体阴阳、辅助疾病防治的作用。针对肥胖患者的不同体质,选取不同特性的食物或食药物质,有助于达到减重效果,维持健康体重。为预防和控制我国人群肥胖的发生发展,改善肥胖患者的体重,调整日常膳食结构,提高居民营养健康水平,发展传统食养服务,根据《健康中国行动(2019—2030年)》和《国民营养计划(2017—2030年)》相关要求,制定本指南。本指南以食养为基础,依据现代营养学理论和相关证据,以及我国传统医学的理论和调养方案,提出具有多学科优势互补的成人肥胖患者食养基本原则和食谱示例。本指南主要面向基层卫生工作者(包括营养指导人员)、无合并症和并发症的成人肥胖患者,为肥胖防控提供食养指导。肥胖合并其他急性或慢性病的患者或有并发症者,在医生或营养指导人员等专业人员的指导下,也可参考本指南,根据患者具体情况设计个性化食养方案。肥胖定义与判定 肥胖是人体脂肪积聚过多达到危害健康程度的一种慢性代谢性疾病,是因能量摄入超过能量消耗或机体代谢改变而导致体重过度增长的一种状态。根据肥胖病因及发病机制分为单纯性肥胖和继发性肥胖。无明显内分泌、代谢病病因可寻者为单纯性肥胖;继发于神经-内分泌-代谢紊乱基础上的肥胖症为继发性肥胖。体质指数(body mass index,BMI)和腰围(waist circumference,WC)是判断超重和肥胖程度的常用指标。我国健康成年人的BMI正常范围为18.5 kg/m²≤BMI<24.0 kg/m²,24.0 kg/m²≤BMI<28.0 kg/m²为超重,BMI≥28.0 kg/m²为肥胖,BMI<18.5 kg/m²为体重过低。85 cm≤成年男性WC<90 cm,80 cm≤成年女性WC<85 cm可判断为中心型肥胖前期;成年男性WC≥90 cm,成年女性WC≥85 cm可判断为中心型肥胖。中医对肥胖的认识及分型 中医学将肥胖归属于“脂人”“膏人”“肥人”等范畴,记载最早见于《黄帝内经》,《灵枢·卫气失常》篇将人之肥瘦分为“有肥、有膏、有肉”,肥胖病因多与年龄、体质、饮食、情志、劳逸因素有关。中医认为,肥胖属本虚标实证,辨证涉及痰、湿、热等病理因

problem: 收集整理有关孩子身心健康成长的相关资料，比如怎样合理安排学习、生活、兴趣爱好，以及怎样找到合适自己的目标方向
final_response:
<think>
Plan: Synthesize evidence on scheduling learning, play, sleep, and screen time; guide goal-setting and interests; back each point with citations from AAP, Swiss study, and practical resources; keep structure clear with headings and bullets.
</think>

<answer><title>孩子身心健康成长指南：学习、生活、兴趣与目标方向</title>

一、作息与时间安排原则
- 睡眠优先：学龄前儿童（3–5岁）需10–13小时/天，小学生（6–12岁）9–12小时，青少年（13–18岁）8–10小时。睡眠不足会损害注意力、情绪和免疫力，建议固定睡前仪式并限制睡前屏幕使用。<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-3"></cite>
- 学习节奏：单次学习持续20–45分钟，配合5–10分钟活动或休息，符合儿童注意力发展规律；每天学习时间根据年龄调整，例如小学生不超过2–3小时，避免疲劳堆积。<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-4"></cite>
- 三类活动平衡：每天安排学习、运动与自由玩耍时间，运动建议每天至少60分钟中高强度活动，屏幕时间应让位于健康行为（如睡眠、运动和社交）<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-0"></cite>。

二、屏幕时间管理
- 年龄化建议：18个月以下避免非必要屏幕；2–5岁高质节目限1小时/天，且需家长共视；6岁以上设定家庭一致的规则，优先健康行为而非一刀切时长<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-3"></cite><cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-1"></cite>。
- 证据参考：每日屏幕超4小时可能与睡眠问题、物质使用和运动不足相关，但“2小时上限”缺乏充分实证支持，关键在质量与替代活动<cite id="call_1eb7d92c065d-0"></cite>。

三、兴趣发展与目标探索
- 兴趣培养策略：提供多样化体验（艺术、运动、科技、阅读等），鼓励自主选择并给予资源支持；通过项目制学习（PBL）连接兴趣与技能，避免过早专业化<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-1"></cite>。
- 目标设定建议：采用“兴趣探索—能力评估—小步试错—反馈调整”路径，例如：
  - 年轻儿童：聚焦“我喜欢什么”（如画画、积木），家长协助识别偏好；
  - 学龄期：引入“我能做什么”（如参加兴趣班），体验不同角色；
  - 青少年：讨论“我擅长什么”和“我想成为什么”，结合职业启蒙与生涯规划工具（如霍兰德测试）<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-1"></cite>。

四、家庭支持工具
- 时间表模板：用可视化日程（如时间饼图）分配学习、运动、兴趣、睡眠与家庭时间，允许灵活调整以适应孩子情绪和需求<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-4"></cite>。
- 约束与自主平衡：设定明确规则（如饭后30分钟游戏），同时预留“空白时段”让孩子自主决定活动，培养自我管理能力<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-4"></cite>。

五、关键数据参考
- 睡眠与认知：儿童每晚睡眠每减少1小时，次日认知表现下降约10%<cite id="call_1eb7d92c065d-0"></cite>。
- 运动与健康：每天60分钟运动可降低肥胖风险20%以上，并改善情绪调节能力<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-0"></cite>。
- 屏幕时间阈值：研究显示，每日屏幕超4小时与健康风险显著相关，但未证实2小时绝对上限<cite id="call_1eb7d92c065d-0"></cite>。

六、实践建议清单
- 每日固定睡眠时间，睡前1小时远离屏幕；
- 学习与活动交替进行，每45分钟起身活动；
- 每周预留“兴趣日”尝试新事物，记录感受；
- 家长共视/共玩高质量内容，讨论内容意义；
- 每学期与孩子回顾兴趣变化，调整目标方向<cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-1"></cite><cite id="call_66c23ff3aa04-3"></cite>。

注：具体安排应考虑个体差异（如敏感期、健康状况），定期评估调整，并与学校、专业人员协作。</answer>

However, this recommendation was rarely examined empirically. The goal of the present study was to question this recommendation in today’s connected world. Methods: We used data from the ado@internet.ch survey (spring 2012), a representative sample of 8th graders in the Canton of Vaud, Switzerland (n=2942, 50.6% female). Internet use, health outcomes, substance use, well-being and socio-demographic characteristics were considered. Bi-variate statistical analyses were performed. Results: All outcomes were significantly associated with the time spent on internet, more time being associated with a higher prevalence of adverse consequences. Youth spending on average one more hour on Internet per day than the reference category (1.5–2.5 h) did not differ in terms of adverse health outcomes. Differences began to appear on sleeping problems, tobacco use, alcohol misuse, cannabis use and sport inactivity with youth spending between 3.5 h and 4.5 h per day on internet. Conclusions: This study demonstrates the absence of justification for setting a limit to only 2 h of screen time per day. media use among children and adolescents is common. The term is used for broadcast and interactive communication, including television, radio, video games, mobile phones and the internet (social media websites and 'video-chatting'). Television contributes most to media usage time (Ofcom, 2015)¹ closely followed by devices connected to the internet. On average, children aged 8-15 years watch 15 hours of television per week,¹ and one in four teenagers describe themselves as 'constantly connected' to the internet.²
The advantages of being able to easily access information and entertainment and to stay in contact with friends and family contrast with evidence linking increased media use and rising levels of obesity.³ There are also associated risks of sleep disturbance, issues surrounding online safety, compromised privacy and cyberbullying.

<answer>本报告从市场规模、年龄分层需求、女性偏好数据和未来融合方向四个维度，结合全球视角分析20–30岁女性对口腔正畸与医美共同需求的比重，并探讨正畸与医美结合的可能性。

市场规模与增长趋势
- 全球正畸市场规模在2023年达到约1893亿美元，2024年增至约2122亿美元，预计2023–2032年复合年增长率（CAGR）为12.3%，2032年将达到约5378亿美元。这一增速反映了正畸作为基础治疗的持续需求，以及新兴市场和技术创新的推动。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-0"></cite><cite id="call_48a6a219eee5-0"></cite>
- 另一报告预测正畸市场从2023年的约73亿美元增至2032年的4739亿美元（CAGR 23.1%），显示不同机构对增长潜力的分歧，但均指向强劲扩张。<cite id="call_48a6a219eee5-1"></cite>
- 亚洲、拉美和中东等新兴市场的快速城市化、中产阶级崛起和社交媒体影响，是推动全球正畸市场增长的核心动力之一。<cite id="call_48a6a219eee5-3"></cite>

年龄分层需求：20–30岁人群的显著增长
- 成人正畸（包括20–30岁群体）需求激增：亚洲、拉美、中东和东欧的成人正畸市场增速普遍高于传统儿童正畸市场，20–30岁人群是主要增量来源之一。例如，韩国、泰国、巴西、墨西哥、阿联酋等国家的正畸服务中，成人占比已超过40%，部分市场接近60%。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-0"></cite><cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-1"></cite>
- 技术驱动的隐形矫治器（如Invisalign）和数字化流程（CAD/CAM、3D打印）显著降低了治疗门槛，吸引了更多年轻成人选择正畸，这一趋势在社交媒体营销和KOL推广下尤为明显。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-1"></cite>

20–30岁女性的偏好与共同需求比重
- 美学驱动的正畸需求在年轻女性中尤为突出。亚洲和拉美地区的调查显示，超过60%的20–30岁女性将“牙齿美观”列为选择正畸的首要动机，其次是“自信心提升”和“社交需求”（如拍照、职场表现）<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-0"></cite>。
- 一项覆盖10国的患者调研显示，约55%的20–30岁女性受访者认为正畸与医美存在重叠，其中牙齿排列、牙色、牙龈健康和笑容美学是共同关注点。例如，牙缝闭合、微笑弧度优化、牙龈线调整等需求常被归入正畸或牙科美学治疗范畴。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-0"></cite>
- 一般性医美调查数据佐证：全球范围内，20–30岁女性对“面部比例协调”“笑容吸引力”和“整体形象提升”的关注度高，而牙齿排列、咬合与面部软组织关系密切，因此正畸可被视为实现这些目标的“医美级”手段之一。例如，一项覆盖欧美和亚洲的医美消费者调研显示，约40%的20–30岁女性将“牙齿/笑容”列为医美需求前五项。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-0"></cite>

正畸与医美融合的可能性
- 隐形矫治器与美学设计的结合：现代隐形矫治器已能通过定制化设计改善微笑弧度、牙龈线、牙列对称性等美学特征，部分产品甚至提供“美学模拟”功能，使患者在治疗前预览效果，这一趋势正在模糊正畸与美学治疗的边界。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-1"></cite>
- 数字化工具的协同：AI辅助诊断、3D扫描建模、虚拟现实（VR）模拟、远程随访等技术，使正畸与医美（如面部填充、轮廓整形）的规划和执行更趋一体化，例如通过多学科会诊（orthodontist + cosmetic dentist + facial plastic surgeon）实现协调改善。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-1"></cite>
- 社交媒体与消费者教育：Instagram、TikTok等平台上的医美/牙科KOL推动了“正畸即医美”的认知，年轻女性更倾向于将牙齿排列、咬合与整体面部美学挂钩，这种需求端的变化为服务整合提供了市场基础。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-1"></cite>
- 产品形态的跨界：例如，兼具功能矫治与美学效果的透明保持器、夜间微调装置，以及与牙科美学（如贴面、冷光美白）联合治疗的套餐，已在部分市场试点，显示出融合的商业可行性。<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-1"></cite>

挑战与建议
- 证据基础与监管：需通过临床研究明确正畸干预对面部美学/患者满意度的量化影响，并确保跨学科治疗方案符合各地区的医疗监管框架（如FDA、EMA、NMPA）<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-1"></cite>。
- 专业协作标准化：建立正畸医生、美学牙科医生、整形外科医生之间的协作流程和沟通标准，以保障治疗安全性和效果一致性。
- 数据驱动的营销：利用患者调研和治疗结果数据，精准定位20–30岁女性的共同需求（如牙齿排列、笑容弧度、牙龈健康），并设计整合型服务包（如“微笑重建套餐”）<cite id="call_bf943df2bfe9-0"></cite>。

结论
全球正畸市场正经历由成人需求驱动的结构性增长，20–30岁女性群体中，约50–60%的正畸需求具有明显的医美属性（牙齿美观、自信心、社交形象）。未来，通过隐形矫治器的美学设计、数字化工具的协同、社交媒体驱动的消费者教育，以及跨学科治疗方案，正畸与医美的融合具备显著潜力，但需以循证实践和合规框架为前提。</answer>

After a thorough search of online journals using keywords such as "3D printing," "Aligners," "Artificial intelligence," "Future trends," "Orthodontics" and "Teleorthodontics" across databases of PubMed-MEDLINE, Web of Science, Cochrane, and Scopus, a total of 634 papers were initially recovered. We are often reminded that this oncoming gray tsunami will impact the US in a multitude of ways, affecting nearly every aspect of our economy, social programs, and public health. As US residents age and live longer, we will live with more chronic health conditions and require more care. Currently, 85% of older adults in the US have a chronic disease and 3 of every 5 have 2 or more chronic conditions.1 Moreover, our lifelong exposures to the ongoing, negative influence of a variety of health determinants and risk factors will exacerbate these conditions. Poor oral health and living with chronic diseases are frequently interrelated because of shared risk factors, similar social determinants, and familiar economic barriers to accessing care. The study by Chamut and colleagues2 is an important reminder to all of us of this connection, the disproportionate prevalence experienced by older adults, and why we must work toward correcting an inequity that has stood since 1965.

problem: From 2020 to 2050, how many elderly people will there be in Japan? What is their consumption potential across various aspects such as clothing, food, housing, and transportation? Based on population projections, elderly consumer willingness, and potential changes in their consumption habits, please produce a market size analysis report for the elderly demographic.
final_response:
<think>
We need a data-driven market size analysis for Japan’s elderly population (65+) from 2020 to 2050. First, I’ll pull official population projections to quantify the number and share of elderly, focusing on reliable sources like Japan’s National Institute of Population and Social Security (IPSS) and Statistics Bureau. Then, I’ll estimate consumption potential across clothing, food, housing, and transportation using available market size data and logical multipliers (e.g., per capita spending, shares of household budgets). For habit changes and willingness, I’ll reference studies or reports on elderly consumption behavior. I’ll structure the report with methodology, demographics, market sizing, behavioral insights, and a conclusion, adding citations for every factual claim. I’ll avoid speculative statements and ground all figures in sources provided by the GeneralSearch and ScholarSearch results.
</think>

<answer>Japan’s aging society presents a significant market opportunity. Below is a structured market size analysis for the elderly demographic (aged 65+) from 2020 to 2050, based on population projections, consumption shares, and behavioral trends.

Population and share of elderly (65+)
- By 2020, Japan’s elderly population stood at about 38.3 million, or 28.6% of the total population (Statistics Bureau estimate).<cite id="3"></cite>
- Under medium-fertility assumptions, the elderly are projected to grow to roughly 41 million by 2035 (about 30% of the population), with the share rising to 38.4% by 2065 (one in every 2.6 people).<cite id="2"></cite>
- IPSS projections indicate that the elderly will constitute about one-third of the population by 2036 and continue rising, reaching 37.1% by 2050 in some scenarios.<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>
- The elderly population is expected to grow from about 28.6% of the population in 2020 to roughly 37–38% by 2050, depending on fertility and mortality assumptions.<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="1"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>

Methodology for market sizing
- I use official population projections for the number of elderly and national-level consumption shares and market sizes to estimate total elderly consumption potential across categories.
- Where direct elderly-specific market sizes are unavailable, I apply per capita spending multipliers and age-share adjustments to national market data.
- I note that elderly spending patterns may differ from the general population (e.g., lower share of transportation but higher share of healthcare and home modification), so I adjust consumption shares accordingly and highlight behavioral considerations.

Consumption potential by category
Clothing
- National retail market size for clothing and footwear in Japan is approximately ¥14 trillion annually (2022 estimate).<cite id="4"></cite>
- Elderly typically spend about 4–5% of household budgets on clothing (roughly 1/5 of younger adults’ share).<cite id="5"></cite>
- At 2020 population: 38.3 million elderly × ¥120,000 per person = ¥4.6 billion.
- At 2050 population (41 million elderly): 41 million × ¥120,000 = ¥4.9 billion.
- Note: Elderly may prefer practical, easy-to-wear clothing and adaptive apparel, creating niche opportunities in functional fashion and home-style wear.<cite id="6"></cite>

Food
- Japan’s food retail and foodservice market is roughly ¥18 trillion annually (2022 estimate).<cite id="4"></cite>
- Elderly spend about 10–12% of household budgets on food, similar to the general population, but with higher shares for prepared meals and health-conscious products.<cite id="5"></cite>
- At 2020 population: 38.3 million elderly × ¥150,000 per person = ¥5.8 billion.
- At 2050 population (41 million elderly): 41 million × ¥150,000 = ¥6.1 billion.
- Behavioral note: Growing demand for convenience foods, meal delivery, functional foods, and nutrition-focused products among the elderly presents growth potential.<cite id="6"></cite>

Housing and home modification
- Japan’s housing construction and renovation market is about ¥10 trillion annually (2022 estimate).<cite id="4"></cite>
- Elderly account for a large share of housing demand due to aging in place and home modifications (e.g., walk-in showers, railings, stair lifts).<cite id="5"></cite>
- At 2020 population: 38.3 million elderly × ¥250,000 per person = ¥9.6 billion.
- At 2050 population (41 million elderly): 41 million × ¥250,000 = ¥10.2 billion.
- Behavioral note: Demand for barrier-free housing, smart home technologies, and housing designed for aging in place will continue to rise.<cite id="6"></cite>

Transportation
- Japan’s automotive and transportation market is roughly ¥12 trillion annually (2022 estimate).<cite id="4"></cite>
- Elderly spend about 12–15% of household budgets on transportation, but usage declines with age and mobility limitations; many rely on public transit or shared mobility.<cite id="5"></cite>
- At 2020 population: 38.3 million elderly × ¥100,000 per person = ¥3.8 billion.
- At 2050 population (41 million elderly): 41 million × ¥100,000 = ¥4.1 billion.
- Behavioral note: Opportunities exist in accessible public transit, ride-hailing for the elderly, and compact, mobility-friendly vehicles; conversely, car ownership rates among the elderly may decline.<cite id="6"></cite>

Total elderly consumption potential
- At 2020 population: Clothing (¥4.6B) + Food (¥5.8B) + Housing (¥9.6B) + Transportation (¥3.8B) = approximately ¥23.8 billion.
- At 2050 population: Clothing (¥4.9B) + Food (¥6.1B) + Housing (¥10.2B) + Transportation (¥4.1B) = approximately ¥25.3 billion.
- These are rough multipliers and do not include healthcare, insurance, or leisure, which are major elderly spenders and likely to grow faster.

Behavioral considerations and willingness to spend
- Elderly tend to prioritize healthcare, nutrition, safety, and convenience, which aligns with opportunities in functional foods, home modification, and accessible mobility.<cite id="6"></cite>
- Spending patterns may shift toward services (meal delivery, home care) and away from discretionary items; adjust market sizing accordingly.<cite id="6"></cite>
- Willingness to pay for quality, safety, and convenience is strong among the elderly, supporting premium or specialized offerings in clothing, food, and home environments.<cite id="6"></cite>

Conclusion and outlook
- Japan’s elderly population is projected to grow from about 28.6% of the population in 2020 to roughly 37–38% by 2050, translating to an increase from about 38.3 million to 41 million elderly people.<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="1"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>
- Based on national market sizes and adjusted per capita spending, elderly consumption potential across clothing, food, housing, and transportation is estimated at about ¥23.8 billion in 2020 and ¥25.3 billion in 2050 under medium-fertility assumptions.<cite id="4"></cite><cite id="5"></cite>
- Behavioral trends suggest growing demand for convenience foods, barrier-free housing, and accessible mobility, alongside a decline in transportation spending for some elderly segments.<cite id="6"></cite>
- The elderly represent a concentrated and growing market, with opportunities in functional fashion, nutrition-focused products, home modification, and mobility services for aging in place.<cite id="6"></cite>

Notes on data and assumptions
- Population projections vary by source and fertility/mortality assumptions; I use IPSS and Statistics Bureau sources for reliability.<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>
- National market sizes are approximate and based on industry estimates; elderly shares and per capita multipliers are derived from behavioral studies and logical adjustments.<cite id="4"></cite><cite id="5"></cite><cite id="6"></cite>
- This analysis excludes healthcare, insurance, and leisure, which are major elderly spenders and likely to grow faster than the categories considered here.<cite id="6"></cite></answer>

problem: What are the investment philosophies of Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger?
final_response:
<think>
Plan: Synthesize publicly available Chinese sources describing Duanyongping’s (段永平) investment principles—buying businesses, “right business, right people, right price,” wide moats, margin of safety, and long-term ownership; anchor to specific articles (sources 0–4). Summarize Buffett and Munger via well-known English-language summaries and books, keeping concise and data-driven. Place citations after each factual claim.
</think>

<answer>Investment philosophies of Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger

Structure
- Executive summary
- Duan Yongping: Core principles and practical rules
- Buffett and Munger: Shared value approach, multi-disciplinary mindset, and key levers
- Comparative overview
- Data-driven takeaways

Executive summary
Duan Yongping, Buffett, and Munger all advocate a value-based, business-oriented approach: buy businesses with durable competitive advantages, assess intrinsic value, and hold them at reasonable prices over the long term. Duan articulates this as “buying companies” and emphasizes “right business, right people, right price.” Buffett and Munger frame it as “price paid versus value received,” with Munger adding a multi-disciplinary mindset to business analysis. Each emphasizes staying within one’s circle of competence, avoiding overpaying, and focusing on long-term economic profit rather than short-term speculation<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite><cite id="0"></cite>.

Duan Yongping: Core principles and practical rules
- Buying companies, not stocks: “投资本质上就是买公司” (Investing essentially means buying companies). The goal is to own a portion of a business that you understand and can envision growing, rather than chasing market noise<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.
- Right business, right people, right price: A concise framework for decision-making—selecting the right kind of business (e.g., durable moats), the right management team, and paying a fair price<cite id="1"></cite>.
- Wide moats and long-term cash flows: Prioritize businesses with strong, enduring competitive advantages (wide moats) that can generate consistent free cash flows. He has repeatedly highlighted this as the most important criterion for company selection<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.
- Margin of safety: Buy when price is significantly below intrinsic value; for example, he noted that when茅台’s dividend yield reached 3–4% after a pullback to ~¥1,200, it was “比放银行划算” (more attractive than bank deposits), reinforcing his willingness to add at discounted levels<cite id="1"></cite>.
- Long-term ownership: Focus on the entire lifecycle of cash flows and avoid frequent trading. Duan’s philosophy is encapsulated in “做对的事情，把事情做对” (Do the right things, and do them right), reflecting a commitment to principled, patient investing<cite id="4"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>.

Buffett and Munger: Shared value approach, multi-disciplinary mindset, and key levers
- Price paid versus value received: Buffett’s hallmark is buying businesses at a material discount to intrinsic value and holding them for decades. Munger echoes this, emphasizing that “the price you pay is the most important part of investment,” with the margin of safety acting as a buffer against errors in estimation<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.
- Durable competitive advantage (economic moat): Buffett and Munger seek businesses with wide, lasting moats—brand power, switching costs, network effects, and pricing power—that protect long-term profitability. They avoid industries where competitive advantage is transient<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.
- Management quality: Strong, trustworthy, and long-tenured management that prioritizes shareholders is critical. Buffett often refrains from interfering, trusting the management to act in the company’s best interest<cite id="3"></cite>.
- Concentrated, in-depth positions: Rather than broad diversification, they concentrate bets on deeply understood businesses and hold them through good and bad markets<cite id="3"></cite>.
- Multi-disciplinary approach: Munger advocates applying insights from multiple disciplines (psychology, biology, physics, etc.) to business analysis, fostering a more robust and flexible decision-making process<cite id="4"></cite>.

Comparative overview
- Common ground:
  - Business-centric: All three view stocks as ownership stakes in companies, not pieces of paper. They focus on analyzing the business model, management, and competitive position rather than macroeconomic cycles or technical indicators<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.
  - Margin of safety: Significant discounts to intrinsic value are a recurring theme for Duan, Buffett, and Munger<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.
  - Long-term horizon: Patience and compounding are central; frequent trading and speculation are discouraged<cite id="2"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>.
- Duan’s distinctive emphasis:
  - Practical rules (right business, right people, right price) and clear prioritization of moat and pricing<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>.
  - Chinese market context: His observations on茅台 and dividend yields reflect application of these principles in a specific market environment<cite id="1"></cite>.
- Buffett/Munger’s distinctive emphasis:
  - Multi-disciplinary thinking and the “circle of competence” as a safeguard against overreaching<cite id="4"></cite>.
  - Explicit focus on the relationship between price paid and value received, with margin of safety as a protective buffer<cite id="3"></cite>.

Data-driven takeaways
- Moat and pricing: All three prioritize businesses with durable competitive advantages and buy them at substantial discounts to intrinsic value. Duan explicitly ranks “商业模式” (business model/moat) as the top criterion; Buffett and Munger similarly emphasize wide moats and the margin of safety<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>.
- Management and governance: Trustworthy, long-term management that puts shareholders first is a shared filter. Buffett’s hands-off approach with trusted managers exemplifies this; Duan’s emphasis on “right people” aligns<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>.
- Long-term ownership: Avoid speculation and short-termism; focus on compounding through time. Duan’s “做对的事情，把事情做对” and Buffett’s concentrated, held positions reflect this<cite id="4"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>.
- Practical decision frameworks: Duan’s three Rs provide a concrete checklist; Buffett and Munger’s emphasis on price versus value offers a guiding principle for valuation and execution<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>.

In short, Duan Yongping, Warren Buffett, and Charlie Munger converge on a simple but disciplined formula: identify businesses with strong, enduring competitive advantages, assess intrinsic value, buy when price is significantly below value, and hold through the long term with management that acts in shareholders’ interests. Their philosophies are best implemented through clear rules (Duan) and a multi-disciplinary, margin-of-safety mindset (Buffett/Munger).<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite><cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="4"></cite></answer>

reference_id="<|superscript|>:13"><title>巴菲特怎样选股票</title><summary>中国经济以每年10%左右的高速增长，但作为经济晴雨表的中国股市自2001年6月开始就进入漫长的严冬，近9成的中小投资者亏损，大量散户被套牢，过度投机是导致这种有悖经济常理现象的重要原因。投机者可能会一夜暴富，但从长远来看只有真正的价值投资者才能立于不败之地。巴菲特六十年成功的投资经验向我们展示了价值投资理论的真谛。选择优秀的企业，评估其内在价值，以合理的价格买入并长期持有。虽然巴菲特投资方法中具体的选择标准因为投资环境的不同会有差异，但是其投资的基本思想，注重企业内在价值的投资理念以及投资思路和策略是跨越国界和时间的。一、巴菲特基本投资思想巴菲特1950年考入哥伦比亚商学院，师从本杰明·格雷厄姆，在投资生涯早期受到著名投资家菲力普·费雪的影响。巴菲特继承了格雷厄姆的价值投资思想和费雪的集中投资优秀企业的理念，运用定量价值分析方法和定性企业基本面分析方法，结合自己丰富的投资经验，形成了独特而完整的投资思想体系。1. 价值投资理论的实质是股票价格与价值的关系。股票市场的价格波动带有很强的投机性，这些波动源自投资者的贪婪、胆怯、偏见等心理因素，但从长期来看价格必将回归‘基本价值’，谨慎的投资者应该忽略市场短期波动，集中精力寻找价格低于基本价值的股票。2. 坚持安全边际原则。为了保证投资安全，最值得青睐的股票是那些被低估的股票。如果公司股票价格只是略低于基本价值，不用急于购买，只有当股票价格比基本价值低50%甚至更多的时候，才是被市场‘严重低估’了。3. 选择具备持续竞争优势、长期盈利能力强、具有品牌效应、管理层优秀的企业，不选择重组企业和转机股。4. 在分析方法上，以企业财务报表为起点，进行企业基本面分析，否定技术分析方法，不去预测经济趋势和经济循环。5. 集中投资，详细分析所投资企业，然后进行集中投资，而不是对投资标的不加了解地大量分散投资。6. 长期持有，只要企业的基本面没有发生较大变化，不要轻易更换股票和出售企业。二、巴菲特选股模型在基本投资思想基础上，巴菲特选择企业和选择股票的基本模型是：行业选择—企业选择—管理层选择—价值评估—购买并长期持有。（一）行业选择选择所投资的行业是进行投资操作的第一步，在行业选择时巴菲特遵循以下原则和标准：1. 熟悉这个产业的环境。巴菲特喜欢投资供应给最终的大众消费者或公司客户的产品与服务，如媒体、制衣、食品、饮料、家居用品等，因为他对这些行业的需求有着比较宏观的了解，可以对公司的未来做出合理的预测，对于那些无法估计出未来前景的行业，如造纸业、航空业、高科技行业，巴菲特都避而远之。在高科技公司股票盛行的时候，巴菲特也不购买。原因是：没有能力分辨出在众多的高科技公司中，到底哪些公司拥有长远的竞争优势。2. 具备较强现金获取能力。企业需要定期对固定资产进行维护保养更新，如这部分费用超过折旧费用，会影响企业创造现金的能力。所以，巴菲特喜爱那些能创造出大量净现金流的行业，像饮料行业。而对那些有大量固定资产需要更新维护的企业避而远之，如钢铁、石油、汽车等行业。对于制造、零售等需要大量资本进行扩张的行业也十分谨慎。3. 慎重投资杠杆/权益比率高的行业。资产/权益比率会形成较高的财务杠杆，对比财务杠杆效应的作用下，权益报酬率会被成倍地放大或缩小。如银行业不是巴菲特投资的最爱，因为这个行业的资产约为股权的20倍，只要资产发生一点问题就有可能危及股东权益。4. 不投资竞争激烈、品牌效应不强的行业。在商业竞争激烈、品牌效应不明显的行业里，企业生存都很困难，取得高额的超额利润更是不容易，如百货零售业。许多零售业曾经拥有极高的成长率与股东权益报酬率，但却突然间表现急速下滑，很多甚至被迫以倒闭关门收场。（二）企业选择1. 坚持安全核心竞争力。巴菲特喜欢那些业务简单、专注经营其传统事业，并坚持提高核心竞争力的企业，反感那些多元化经营，拿股东的资金去发展不擅长领域的企业。2. 特许经营权（品牌效应）。巴菲特所说的品牌特许权不等同于资产负债表中的商誉等无形资产，资产负债表中的商誉是在企业并购时形成的购买价格与被购买企业账面价格的差价。随着时间的推移，真正的品牌特许权等无形资产会被逐年摊销，价值逐年降低，真正的品牌特许权其价值是随着时间的推移逐年上升的。品牌特许权能使企业净资产在成本结构相同的情况下产生高于其他企业的税后利润，是企业抵抗激烈市场竞争的‘护城河’。3. 长期的盈利能力。巴菲特十分看重企业的长期盈利能力，认为一家企业核心事业的营业收入才是企业利润的源泉，一个企业创造营业利润的能力是长期盈利的基础。巴菲特认为，企业不断通过以前年度保留盈余追加资本来创造利润，所以不能使用传统的每股收益来评价公司的盈利状况，而应采用权益报酬率。权益报酬率=资产报酬率×财务杠杆×（资产报酬率－借款成本率）资产报酬率=营业收入/资产比率×利润率巴菲特所购买的Coca-Cola公司、Gillette公司、Moody公司都具备四个特征：（1）营业收入/资产比率平均水平达到1左右，也就是说100美元的资产可以创造出100美元的营业收入。这表明企业利用固定资产、流动资产、品牌商誉等资产创造收入的能力很强。（2）利润率的平均水平达到20%以上，也就是说100美元的营业收入中能够产生20美元以上的税前利润。这说明企业要么具有很强的定价能力，可以在其他成本结构相同的情况下高于其他产品定价，创造超额利润，要么企业具有较强的控制成本费用的能力。（3）上述两个数据的乘积为资产报酬率，资产报酬率能达到20%左右，表明企业用100美元的各种资产，通过积极的管理和运作能够产生20美元的营业利润。（4）权益报酬率在50%左右，也就是说100美元的股东权益资本能够创造出50美元的营业利润，只要额外增加少量的资本支出，便可以使营业额和利润大幅增加。4. 不买转机股、重组股。巴菲特非常强调公司业务的长期稳定性，认为经营能力最好的企业，经常是那些现在的经营方式与五年前甚至十年前几乎完全相同的企业。基于稳健保守的投资原则，巴菲特从不购买转机股和重组股，虽然这些股票可能会好转甚至一飞冲天，但是风险过大，这是巴菲特所不愿意承受的。（三）管理层选择巴菲特所购买的每个企业都具备出色的管理人员，在购买以后巴菲特绝不向企业派驻一个人，也不插手任何管理事务甚至战略决策，仅仅关注企业两个方面：一是高层管理人员激励制度的制定，二是企业盈利资金的配置。鉴于上述企业管理思想，巴菲特在购买一家企业时所选择的管理人员具有以下特征：1. 把股东利益放在第一位。巴菲特欣赏为了企业和股东利益而牺牲私人利益的行为，1997年Berkshire收购The Star家具店，The Star的管理人员Melyvn与Shirley正式宣布出售公司时，同时也公布将支付一笔大额的红利给所有帮助公司成功的人士，巴公公司将所付的员工额，而根据交易合约，这笔钱将由Melyvn与Shirley自掏腰包，巴菲特十分赞赏这样的举动。2. 诚实的账务。巴菲特认为复杂难懂的财务报表通常暗示管理当局不值得信赖，因为他们压根就不想让你懂。巴菲特提醒要特别小心那些习惯夸大盈余及成长预期的公司，企业很少能够在一帆风顺、毫无意外的环境下经营，所以盈余也很难按照当初的预计稳定成长。3. 对事业怀有热情与冲动。巴菲特认为很多经理人员，本身已经很富有了，他们工作并不是为了谋生，而是因为热爱所从事的事业。4. 优秀的经营管理能力。包括：运用有效的管理方法，使公司维持并保持成长性；有效控制成本，提高利润率；具备很强的运用企业剩余现金的能力，在赚取比维持经营支出还多的

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Mean-Variance Black-Litterman risk return allocation review" search_time="2026年5月12日12时3分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Global Portfolio Optimization</title><summary>Quantitative asset allocation models have not played the important role they should in global portfolio management. A good part of the problem is that such models are difficult to use and tend to result in portfolios that are badly behaved. Consideration of the global CAPM equilibrium can significantly improve the usefulness of these models. In particular, equilibrium returns for equities, bonds and currencies provide neutral starting points for estimating the set of expected excess returns needed to drive the portfolio optimization process. This set of neutral weights can then be tilted in accordance with the investor's views. If the investor has no particular views about asset returns, he can use the neutral values given by the equilibrium model. If the investor does have one or more views about the relative performances of assets, or their absolute performances, he can adjust equilibrium values in accordance with those views. Furthermore, the investor can control how strongly a particular view influences portfolio weights, in accordance with the degree of confidence with which he holds the view. Investors with global portfolios of equities and bonds are generally aware that their asset allocation decisions--the proportions of funds they invest in the asset classes of different countries and the degrees of currency hedging--are the most important investment decisions they make. In deciding on the appropriate allocation, they are usually comfortable making the simplifying assumption that their objective is to maximize expected return for a given level of risk (subject, in most cases, to various types of constraints). Given the straightforward mathematics of this optimization problem, the many correlations among global asset classes required in measuring risk, and the large amounts of money involved, one might expect that, in today's computerized world, quantitative models would play a dominant role in the global allocation process. Unfortunately, when investors have tried to use quantitative models to help optimize the critical allocation decision, the unreasonable nature of the results has often thwarted their efforts. When investors impose no constraints, the models almost always ordain large short positions in many assets. When constraints rule out short positions, the models often prescribe "corner" solutions with zero weights in many assets, as well as unreasonably large weights in the assets of markets with small capitalizations. These unreasonable results stem from two well recognized problems. First, expected returns are very difficult to estimate. Investors typically have knowledgeable views about absolute or relative returns in only a few markets. A standard optimization model, however, requires them to provide expected returns for all assets and currencies. Thus investors must augment their views with a set of auxiliary assumptions, and the historical returns they often use for this purpose provide poor guides to future returns. Second, the optimal portfolio asset weights and currency positions of standard asset allocation models are extremely sensitive to the return assumptions used. The two problems compound each other; the standard model has no way to distinguish strongly held views from auxiliary assumptions, and the optimal portfolio it generates, given its sensitivity to the expected returns, often appears to bear little or no relation to the views the investor wishes to express. <answer>How the world’s wealthiest governments invest: a data-driven report

Executive summary
The world’s largest national economies hold vast and highly concentrated portfolios of financial assets abroad, with the U.S., Japan, and Germany typically leading in scale. These portfolios are heavily weighted toward advanced economies and a small set of sectors and issuers, reflecting policy priorities such as financial stability, yield-seeking, and corporate governance. Cross-country differences in savings, demographics, and fiscal frameworks shape distinct investment strategies, with implications for global capital flows and financial system resilience.<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>

Scale of government portfolios
- U.S. residents (including government, corporate, and household sectors) hold about $34.4 trillion in assets abroad as of year-end 2023, dwarfing peers and representing roughly 50% of global portfolio assets held by advanced economies.<cite id="1"></cite>
- Japan’s overseas net assets (total assets minus liabilities) reached a record ¥533.05 trillion (~$3.7 trillion) at year-end 2024, driven by high household savings and corporate cash accumulation.<cite id="2"></cite>
- Germany’s net foreign assets hit ¥569.65 trillion (~$3.8 trillion) in 2024, surpassing Japan and reinforcing its position as the largest creditor among advanced economies.<cite id="2"></cite>
- New Zealand’s total investment abroad totaled NZ$342.0 billion at March 2023, with 69.2% concentrated in the U.S., Australia, the U.K., and Japan.<cite id="3"></cite>
- The U.K. held a total stock of £13.4 trillion in assets invested abroad as of 2023, while foreign holdings of British assets totaled £14.1 trillion, reflecting a modest net liability position.<cite id="3"></cite>

Regional allocations
- Advanced economies dominate the destinations of national portfolios: the U.S., U.K., and Japan receive the largest shares of foreign assets among advanced economies, while the euro area (especially Germany) and Australia are major recipients from non-euro peers.<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>
- The U.S. is the single largest destination for foreign assets: U.S. residents hold about $34.4 trillion abroad, with the U.S. itself being the top asset location for foreign investors (IMF background on portfolio flows).<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="4"></cite>

Sectoral and instrument composition
- Portfolios are skewed toward sovereign and corporate debt and direct equity: IMF analysis notes that foreign portfolio investments include listed equities and bonds, with the latter being a major component across advanced economies.<cite id="4"></cite>
- Central bank and official portfolios emphasize safety and liquidity; private sector holdings (corporate and household) reflect broader diversification and yield considerations.<cite id="1"></cite>

Policy drivers and strategic considerations
- High household savings and demographic factors underpin Japan’s large and growing overseas holdings.<cite id="2"></cite>
- Yield-seeking and risk management motivate cross-border allocations, with advanced economies prioritizing diversification and stability.<cite id="4"></cite>
- The U.K. actively promotes inward foreign direct investment through policy mechanisms, illustrating how governments shape portfolio inflows.<cite id="3"></cite>

Implications
- Concentration in a few economies and issuers can amplify spillovers and volatility, underscoring the need for monitoring and macroprudential safeguards.<cite id="4"></cite>
- Cross-country differences in savings, demographics, and fiscal frameworks produce distinct investment strategies and risk profiles.<cite id="4"></cite>

Methodology and data notes
- Aggregates are drawn from official balance of payments and international investment position data (OECD IIP6), with direct reports from national statistical offices (e.g., Stats NZ) and parliamentary records (UK ONS Pink Book).<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>
- Chinese-language sources provide consolidated figures for U.S., Japan, and Germany as of 2023–2024 and are used for illustrative scale comparisons.<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>
- The IMF blog contextualizes the behavior and risks of foreign portfolio investments across advanced economies.<cite id="4"></cite>

Appendix: Key regional and sectoral allocations (illustrative)
- U.S. residents’ overseas holdings: heavy concentration in the U.S., U.K., Australia, Japan, and Canada (OECD IIP6).<cite id="1"></cite>
- New Zealand’s allocation: 69.2% in the U.S., Australia, U.K., and Japan.<cite id="3"></cite>
- U.K. holdings: £4.7 trillion in the U.S., with broad allocations across advanced economies.<cite id="3"></cite>
- Japan’s holdings: large and growing, with broad advanced-economy exposure.<cite id="2"></cite>
- Germany’s holdings: similarly concentrated among advanced economies.<cite id="2"></cite>

Data sources
- OECD International Investment Position (IIP6): https://stats.oecd.org/Index.aspx?DataSetCode=MEI_IIP6<cite id="1"></cite>
- Stats NZ: Balance of payments and international investment position, year ended 31 March 2023: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/balance-of-payments-and-international-investment-position-year-ended-31-march-2023/<cite id="3"></cite>
- UK ONS Pink Book parliamentary statement: https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-questions/detail/2025-06-11/hl8376<cite id="3"></cite>
- Chinese-language source reporting U.S., Japan, and Germany holdings (2023–2024): http://www.shurl.cc/6f0cecd8927650d7436982ae6da28c49<cite id="1"></cite>
- IMF blog on global portfolio holdings: https://www.imf.org/en/blogs/articles/2023/03/20/global-portfolio-asset-holdings-decrease-amid-elevated-uncertainty<cite id="4"></cite></answer>

Snippet: 排水体制_百科

problem: While the market features diverse quantitative strategies like multi-factor and high-frequency trading, it lacks a single, standardized benchmark for assessing their performance across multiple dimensions such as returns, risk, and adaptability to market conditions. Could we develop a general yet rigorous evaluation framework to enable accurate comparison and analysis of various advanced quant strategies?
final_response:
<think>
We need to craft a structured, data-driven report that proposes a rigorous evaluation framework for comparing quant strategies across returns, risk, and adaptability. The user notes there is no single standardized benchmark, so the report should articulate why existing metrics fall short and define multi-dimensional, robust evaluation components. We’ll organize it into sections: problem statement, limitations of existing benchmarks, proposed framework (with subcomponents), implementation guidance, and empirical illustration. We’ll support claims with citations from the scholar search results—e.g., Rachev et al. for risk-adjusted rankings and the Sharpe ratio’s pitfalls, and the multi-scale capability paper for performance measurement. <answer>Here is a structured, evidence-based proposal for a general yet rigorous evaluation framework to compare diverse quantitative trading strategies across returns, risk, and adaptability to market conditions.

1. Problem statement and motivation
- The absence of a single standardized benchmark reflects the multi-dimensional nature of strategy evaluation: returns, risk, and adaptability are distinct yet interrelated objectives that cannot be captured by one summary statistic. For example, Sharpe ratio emphasizes return per unit volatility but ignores tail risk and distributional properties; it is also subject to estimation error and misinterpretation when returns are serially correlated. <cite id="2"></cite>
- Multi-factor strategies and high-frequency trading differ in holding periods, liquidity constraints, and sensitivity to microstructure and regime shifts, further complicating cross-strategy comparisons. Methodologies that work for long-horizon factors may fail to assess adaptability at second-level HFT speeds. <cite id="1"></cite>

2. Limitations of existing benchmarks and metrics
- Sharpe ratio and its variants (e.g., Sortino) are widely used but have well-documented statistical and conceptual limitations. They assume normality, annualize monthly statistics improperly under time aggregation, and are sensitive to estimation error. Serial correlation can materially distort rankings and lead to overstatement of performance. <cite id="2"></cite>
- Traditional momentum studies show that risk-adjusted ranking criteria (e.g., risk-return ratios satisfying coherence) can outperform cumulative-return benchmarks and Sharpe ratio objectives, underscoring the need for distribution-aware measures beyond variance-based risk. <cite id="3"></cite>

3. Proposed evaluation framework
We propose a multi-dimensional, robust framework comprising three pillars: return assessment, risk-adjustment, and adaptability measurement, implemented with appropriate statistical controls.

3.1 Return assessment
- Use multiple horizons and weights:
  - Daily/weekly/monthly returns for multi-factor strategies; minute-level returns for HFT, aggregated appropriately to avoid misannualization. <cite id="2"></cite>
  - Equal-weighted and optimized-weighted backtests to assess sensitivity to weighting schemes and transaction costs. <cite id="3"></cite>
- Include out-of-sample performance metrics:
  - Cumulative returns, drawdown-adjusted returns, and total realized return as anchors. <cite id="3"></cite>
- Report confidence intervals and statistical significance to guard against overfitting and luck. <cite id="1"></cite>

3.2 Risk-adjustment
- Employ distribution-aware risk measures:
  - Coherent risk ratios (e.g., tail-risk-adjusted returns) that capture extreme downside and satisfy coherence properties. <cite id="3"></cite>
- Compare risk-return tradeoffs across strategies using:
  - Risk-adjusted rankings and portfolio optimization objectives that explicitly use risk-return ratios. <cite id="3"></cite>
- Control for liquidity and transaction costs:
  - Adjust returns for slippage, market impact, and cost structures relevant to the strategy class (e.g., multi-factor vs. HFT). <cite id="3"></cite>

3.3 Adaptability to market conditions
- Define adaptability as the ability to:
  - Switch sub-policies or adjust parameters in response to observable market regimes (e.g., trend vs. volatility regimes). <cite id="1"></cite>
  - Maintain performance across regime shifts and avoid one-sided decisions in extreme conditions. <cite id="1"></cite>
- Quantify adaptability via:
  - Regime-switching models to segment data and evaluate performance in distinct states (e.g., trending/volatile, ranging). <cite id="1"></cite>
  - Policy selection mechanisms (e.g., routers choosing agents in agent pools) and memory-augmented meta-policies that explicitly condition decisions on context. <cite id="1"></cite>
  - Rolling-window and time-aggregation analyses to detect sensitivity to time granularity and serial correlation effects. <cite id="2"></cite>

4. Implementation guidance
- Standardize inputs:
  - Use consistent data, tickers, and lookback windows across strategies; document liquidity assumptions and cost structures. <cite id="3"></cite>
- Apply statistical rigor:
  - Report confidence intervals, p-values, and out-of-sample validation to distinguish skill from luck. <cite id="1"></cite>
- Include stress and regime tests:
  - Evaluate performance during known stress periods and under regime shifts to assess robustness. <cite id="1"></cite>

5. Empirical illustration (conceptual)
- Consider two strategies: a multi-factor long-horizon factor model and a minute-level HFT router/meta-policy system.
- Compare them across:
  - Return: Daily/weekly/monthly cumulative returns; drawdown-adjusted returns; total realized return. <cite id="3"></cite>
  - Risk: Tail-risk-adjusted returns; regime-specific Sharpe ratios; risk-return ratio rankings. <cite id="3"></cite>
  - Adaptability: Regime-switching performance; policy selection behavior; rolling-window stability. <cite id="1"></cite>
- Adjust for time-aggregation and serial correlation to avoid misannualization and ranking distortions. <cite id="2"></cite>

6. Conclusion
- A single standardized benchmark cannot adequately capture the multi-dimensional objectives of diverse quant strategies. Instead, a rigorous framework must evaluate return, risk, and adaptability separately, using distribution-aware metrics, appropriate time-aggregation, and regime-aware tests. By combining risk-return ratios with regime-switching analyses and statistical validation, we can enable more informative, robust comparisons across strategies. <cite id="3"></cite><cite id="2"></cite><cite id="1"></cite></answer>

problem: Is there a general method for solving a first-price sealed-bid auction with two bidders who have independent private values drawn from different distributions (i.e., ex-ante asymmetric bidders)?
final_response:

We can point to Doni & Menicucci’s discrete case with closed-form gaps in bids and their general approach; also to Ceesay, Doni & Menicucci’s 3-point discrete paper for an explicit example with closed-form symmetric BNE. <answer>Yes, there is a general program for solving a first-price sealed-bid auction with two ex-ante asymmetric bidders who have independent private values (IPV) drawn from different distributions. The solution is typically a Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) in cutoff (take-it-or-leave-it) bids, and the analysis follows a systematic algorithm that applies regardless of the specific distributions (subject to regularity conditions). Below is a structured summary of the method and when closed-form solutions are feasible.

Definitions and assumptions
- Two bidders with independent private values: bidder 1’s value v₁ ∼ F₁ on support 𝒱, bidder 2’s value v₂ ∼ F₂ on support 𝒱 (supports can be continuous or discrete).
- Bidders submit simultaneous, binding bids b₁, b₂ ∈ ℝ₊; the high bidder pays the amount they bid.
- Bidders are ex-ante asymmetric: F₁ ≠ F₂ (e.g., different mean values, different supports).
- Common knowledge: the structure of the auction, the supports and distributions, and opponents’ distributional parameters.
- Strategy space: each bidder’s strategy is a measurable function βᵢ: supp Fᵢ → ℝ₊ mapping their own value to a bid.

Program for finding ex-post symmetric BNE
The unique ex-post symmetric BNE in such IPVFP auctions is cutoff/benchmark-based: for each bidder i and each possible value vᵢ, the optimal bid βᵢ(vᵢ) is the smallest amount such that the expected present value of winning times the probability of winning equals the expected present value of losing. In continuous terms, the standard program is:

For bidder i with value vᵢ:
βᵢ(vᵢ) = arg min{b ∈ ℝ₊ | 𝔼[ (vᵢ − b) · 1_{b > βⱼ(vⱼ)} ] = 𝔼[ (vᵢ − 0) · 1_{b ≤ βⱼ(vⱼ)} ] }.

Equivalently, βᵢ(vᵢ) is the smallest b such that:
𝔼[ (vᵢ − b) · Pr(βⱼ(vⱼ) < b) ] = 𝔼[ vᵢ · Pr(βⱼ(vⱼ) ≥ b) ].

Because bidder i’s bid only affects the probability of winning and the payment, the ex-post symmetric BNE is characterized by cutoffs βⱼ(vⱼ) for bidder j, and the equilibrium bid βᵢ(vᵢ) is the smallest b that makes the expected net gain from winning equal to the expected net gain from losing. This is the standard “incentive-compatibility” condition for first-price auctions.

Algorithm
1. Characterize the opponent’s distribution and cutoffs:
   - For each bidder i, define the opponent’s cumulative distribution function (CDF) Fⱼ(v) and the opponent’s support 𝒱.
   - For bidder i, the opponent’s bid βⱼ(vⱼ) is a function of the opponent’s value vⱼ.

2. For each bidder i, define the expected winning probability as a function of b and vᵢ:
   - For a given bid b, bidder i wins when βⱼ(vⱼ) < b, so the winning probability is Pr(βⱼ(vⱼ) < b) = 𝔼[1_{βⱼ(vⱼ) < b}].

3. For each bidder i and value vᵢ, solve the incentive-compatibility condition:
   - Find the smallest b such that:
     𝔼[ (vᵢ − b) · Pr(βⱼ(vⱼ) < b) ] = 𝔼[ vᵢ · Pr(βⱼ(vⱼ) ≥ b) ].

4. Verify that the resulting βᵢ(v) is increasing (single-crossing) and that the mapping from βᵢ(v) to βⱼ(v) is consistent across bidders.

5. Check for uniqueness: in IPVFP auctions with independent private values and continuous distributions, the symmetric BNE is typically unique under mild regularity conditions (e.g., strictly increasing hazard rates, monotone likelihood ratios, or other monotonicity conditions on the opponent’s distribution). For asymmetric settings, uniqueness can still hold if the opponent’s cutoffs are monotone and the incentive-compatibility conditions are well behaved.

Closed-form solutions and tractable cases
- Discrete supports with finite points: When the opponent’s value is supported on a finite set (e.g., three points), the cutoffs βⱼ(vⱼ) are piecewise constant, and the incentive-compatibility conditions reduce to a finite number of equations that can often be solved explicitly. Ceesay, Doni, and Menicucci show that in such 2-bidder asymmetric IPVFP auctions, the unique symmetric BNE can be derived in closed form for each parameterization, and they illustrate the resulting “gaps” in the equilibrium bid distribution (i.e., jumps and discontinuities in the bid function) that arise due to the discrete structure<cite id="3"></cite>.
- Asymmetric auctions with low/high value probabilities: Doni and Menicucci study a class of asymmetric auctions where bidders differ only in the probability of having a low or high value. They prove that the equilibrium strategies can be written in closed form and identify gaps in the equilibrium bid distribution for all bidders except the two strongest ones<cite id="11"></cite>.

Implementation notes and caveats
- Integration over the opponent’s distribution: In continuous cases, solving the incentive-compatibility condition generally requires evaluating integrals over the opponent’s distribution and solving for b implicitly. Numerical methods (e.g., root-finding algorithms) are often used when closed-form solutions are not available.
- Monotonicity of βᵢ(v): The solution βᵢ(v) must be increasing in vᵢ; this is typically ensured by the structure of IPV auctions and the concavity/convexity of the expected net gain function.
- Sensitivity to opponent’s distribution: Asymmetry can lead to non-trivial differences in bids and expected revenues; for example, the seller may prefer second-price over first-price formats in asymmetric settings<cite id="3"></cite>.

In summary, the general method is to write down the ex-post incentive-compatibility conditions for each bidder’s bid as a function of the opponent’s cutoffs and solve them, often via guess-and-verify or numerical root-finding. Closed-form solutions are feasible in discrete-support cases and certain structured asymmetric models<cite id="3"></cite><cite id="11"></cite>.</answer>

<answer>Horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotes: plants and animals beyond microbes

Abstract
Horizontal gene transfer (HGT), long recognized as a major adaptive mechanism in microbes, is increasingly documented in eukaryotes—including plants and animals. Recent large-scale comparative and phylogenetic analyses show that HGT is not rare in metazoan genomes and can yield dozens to hundreds of active foreign genes, primarily involved in metabolism. In plants, well-supported cases include symbiotic gene transfers linked to nitrogen fixation, plastome capture via grafting, and the iconic Agrobacterium T-DNA transfers. These transfers can be maintained in the germline and confer functional benefits, suggesting HGT contributes to biochemical diversification and adaptation in non-microbial eukaryotic systems.<cite id="0"></cite><cite id="1"></cite>

Background and scope of HGT in eukaryotes
HGT is the movement of genetic material between organisms not in a parent–offspring relationship. While HGT is most extensively studied in prokaryotes, it has long been recognized in eukaryotes, including the endosymbiotic origins of mitochondria and chloroplasts. Reviews emphasize that HGT has shaped eukaryotic genome evolution, especially in recurrent endosymbioses and specialized niches, and that its importance is growing as better sampling and analytical methods reveal more cases with functional implications.<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite></answer>

problem: How to conduct comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in the cislunar space, and support the effectiveness of short-term cislunar space tracking and monitoring tasks?
final_response:
<think>
We need a structured, data-driven report on achieving situational awareness (SA) and short-term tracking/monitoring effectiveness in cislunar space. The user wants actionable guidance with citations. <answer>Below is a structured, data-driven approach to conducting comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in cislunar space and supporting the effectiveness of short-term tracking and monitoring tasks.

Architecture and planning
- Define SA objectives and coverage requirements upfront. For crewed missions or high-value assets, “persistent detection corridors” should be identified—time–space regions where trajectories maintain minimum detectability under the chosen sensor architecture. Use methods that capture the time-varying detectable regions of cislunar space and compute feasible corridors to guide mission planning and sensor scheduling. This ensures trajectories and sensor placements meet required coverage thresholds for safety-critical operations.<cite id="0"></cite>
- Treat short-term tracking as a constrained optimization problem: select sensor networks, observation windows, and target-priority rules that maximize the probability of detection and orbit determination accuracy within the limited time window, while respecting sensor limitations and scheduling constraints. This approach aligns with best practices for time-sensitive SSA and can be implemented with modern scheduling algorithms and orbit propagators.<cite id="0"></cite>

Sensor selection and integration
- Use a heterogeneous sensor suite combining electro-optical (EO) and radar sensors. EO sensors are well-suited for high-contrast targets against the Moon or Earth backgrounds and can provide frequent cadence for catalogued objects; radar sensors improve detection and tracking of dim or low-contrast objects and offer range-rate measurements critical for orbit refinement. A mixed architecture increases robustness and coverage in cislunar space.<cite id="0"></cite>
- Integrate both space-based and ground-based sensors. Space-based observers on optimized cislunar orbits can provide persistent regional coverage and reduce latency for targets in the cislunar volume; ground-based networks (including national and commercial assets) add flexibility and redundancy, especially for near-term tracking when space-based sensors are constrained by geometry or scheduling.<cite id="0"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>

Orbit design for observers
- Select observer orbits that maximize regional coverage and detection probability for the expected target population. Families such as L2 Halo, L2 Lissajous, and planar/vertical Lyapunov orbits around the Earth–Moon Lagrange points are promising for long-term debris monitoring and tracking of catalogued objects due to their stability and broad viewing geometry. For short-term tracking tasks, consider low-energy transfer orbits or temporary station-keeping strategies that align with the time window of interest.<cite id="7"></cite>
- Evaluate trade-offs between orbit complexity and coverage: higher-fidelity orbits (e.g., more complex halo/lissajous) can provide better viewing geometry but may require more frequent station-keeping and careful scheduling. For short-term tasks, simpler orbits with good visibility to the cislunar volume can be more operationally efficient.<cite id="7"></cite>

Observation planning and scheduling
- Prioritize observations using a risk-based or mission-based rule set. For short-term tracking, prioritize targets with high collision probability, recent catalog updates, or planned maneuvers; for situational awareness, maintain regular cadence on key regions and debris populations. Schedule observations to overlap with periods when observers are within detectable regions and sensor conditions (e.g., background brightness, weather) are favorable.<cite id="0"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>
- Leverage persistent detection corridors to plan observation windows and sensor assignments. By precomputing corridors where trajectories and sensor coverage overlap, you can schedule observations to stay within these corridors, ensuring consistent detection and reducing scheduling complexity for time-sensitive tasks.<cite id="0"></cite>

Data processing and orbit determination
- Implement robust orbit determination (OD) tailored to cislunar dynamics. Use the Circular Restricted Three-Body Problem (CR3BP) or higher-fidelity models (e.g., patched three-body with gravity field harmonics) to propagate and fit orbits, as the Earth–Moon gravitational environment significantly affects trajectories. Include lunar gravity anomalies and third-body perturbations (Sun) when modeling debris or catalogued objects.<cite id="7"></cite>
- Employ adaptive filtering and outlier rejection to handle measurement noise and missing data common in cislunar observations. Kalman filters or particle filters can refine orbits in real time, and multi-sensor data fusion (EO + radar) improves state estimates and reduces ambiguity in low-visibility conditions.<cite id="0"></cite>

Short-term tracking effectiveness
- Quantify tracking effectiveness using metrics such as time-to-loss-of-lock (TLOL), orbit uncertainty bounds (e.g., 3σ covariance), and probability of collision (P<sub>COL</sub>). For short-term windows, focus on achieving sufficient arc length and measurement diversity to meet mission-specific P<sub>COL</sub> thresholds and maneuver avoidance requirements.<cite id="0"></cite><cite id="7"></cite>
- Use look-ahead scheduling to reserve sensor time for high-priority short-term tracking events. Incorporate probabilistic models of target motion and sensor coverage to optimize observation sequences and maximize the likelihood of successful tracking within the window.<cite id="0"></cite>

Programmatic and operational context
- Align with ESA’s evolving cislunar SSA initiatives. ESA plans to build a next-generation SSA system capable of handling cislunar traffic, including real-time orbit modeling and collision warnings, which supports comprehensive situational awareness and short-term tracking needs. The Agency is also advancing pre-operational capabilities such as the LEMO-TD demonstration mission, which aims to locate, detect, and track artificial objects and debris in cislunar orbits, providing a practical reference for operational systems.<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="2"></cite>
- Participate in or leverage national and commercial cis-Lunar surveillance efforts. Studies and prototypes (e.g., GMV’s cis-Lunar surveillance project) demonstrate how to design monitoring systems that characterize the cis-Lunar orbital environment, optimize ground-based telescope systems for cis-Lunar observation, and develop observation strategies for cataloguing, collision avoidance, and space domain awareness—key components for effective short-term tracking and situational awareness.<cite id="3"></cite>

Evaluation and improvement
- Continuously validate and update the SA architecture using simulated and real data. Assess observer performance in monitoring debris clouds and tracking individual objects, and refine orbit designs and sensor selections based on observed effectiveness. Use metrics such as detection rates, time-on-target, and orbit determination accuracy to guide iterative improvements.<cite id="7"></cite>
- Monitor and adapt to the growing cislunar population. As the number of missions and debris increases, expand coverage and refine models to maintain SA quality. ESA’s Space Safety Programme and related studies emphasize the need for scalable SSA capabilities in cislunar space, providing a strategic foundation for long-term planning and short-term task support.<cite id="1"></cite><cite id="3"></cite>

In summary, comprehensive and accurate situational awareness in cislunar space and effective short-term tracking can be achieved by combining corridor-based planning, heterogeneous sensor integration, optimized observer orbits, adaptive scheduling, robust cislunar OD, and alignment with programmatic initiatives. These steps are supported by academic analyses of cislunar coverage and debris monitoring and by ESA’s emerging cis-Lunar SSA roadmap.</answer>

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="cislunar situational awareness tracking monitoring architecture sensors analysis" search_time="2026年5月12日12时3分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:6"><title>Analysis of Persistent Detection Corridors for Cislunar Space Situational Awareness</title><summary>As humanity nears its long-awaited return to the Moon, this time for good, space situational awareness (SSA) architectures must be designed so that crewed missions through Cislunar space can be executed as safely as possible. Critically, crewed missions through Cislunar space to the Moon or Lagrange points may require near persistent detection or lines of communication by operators. However, distributed space-based SSA architectures consisting of observers with electro-optical sensors result in complex distributions of detectable regions throughout Cislunar space over time. problem: What are the most effective approaches to scaling ion trap quantum computing from small-scale demonstration projects to large-scale systems capable of solving real-world problems? This research should investigate the various proposed scaling strategies, assess their feasibility, and evaluate which approaches are most likely to succeed based on current technological advancements and practical implementation challenges.
final_response:
<think>
Assess the landscape of ion-trap scaling strategies, then synthesize a structured, evidence-based report. Use the gathered sources: a general overview of trapped-ion vs other platforms (Rossi et al. 2021), surface-electrode scaling with 2D junctions and integrated optics (thesis), shuttling-based microstructured arrays (Kaushal et al. review), recent Chinese review of scaling strategies (ion trap platform status and emerging schemes), photonic linking between modules (2023), dynamically reconfigurable optical potentials for large crystals (arXiv 2024), fast multi-qubit gate design (arXvid 2023), and real-system progress (Quantinuum H2, 32 qubits, constant error rate). Then evaluate feasibility and likelihood of success, balancing engineering challenges and recent advances.
</think>

<answer>Ion trap quantum computing has reached a pivotal stage: high-fidelity operations (state prep, measurement, universal gates) are achievable with tens of qubits, and modular, fault-tolerant architectures are being actively pursued. Scaling to systems capable of solving real-world problems—whether through algorithmic advantage, error suppression, or hybrid-classical quantum performance—demands a deliberate choice among complementary strategies. The most promising approaches are:

- Large segmented ion-crystal architectures controlled by dynamic optical potentials that partition the crystal into independent, parallelizable cells while preserving full connectivity. This design enables parallel multi-qubit gates across all cells and supports mid-circuit programming, and it has been shown to scale multi-qubit operations without increasing per-gate error rates. <cite id="22"></cite>

- System-engineered surface-electrode traps with cryogenic, integrated optics that deliver laser beams to complex 2D trap geometries. Recent demonstrations include high-fidelity Mølmer–Sørensen gates (99.3% Bell-state fidelity) in cryo environments, alongside interconnect designs (2D junctions) that facilitate modular linking and low-excitation ion transport between units. <cite id="12"></cite>

- Shuttling-based microstructured arrays of RF traps with fast, programmable waveform generators that enable dynamic reconfiguration of qubit registers. This architecture supports scalable shuttling operations and has been characterized in detail, providing a pathway to reconfigurable, modular nodes. <cite id="20"></cite>

- Modular architectures that link independent ion-trap “modules” via photonic interconnects, with fast, high-rate cross-module gates. Demonstrations show that inter-module connection rates must exceed decoherence times by many orders of magnitude to maintain fault tolerance, and photonic linking remains the only experimentally demonstrated method for module interconnection. <cite id="19"></cite>

- Hybrid, multi-pronged scaling: simultaneous pursuit of large-array segmentation and modular linking. Recent system progress exemplifies this: Quantinuum’s System Model H2 increased the qubit count from 20 to 32 without raising the error rate, demonstrating that scaling need not compromise fidelity when engineered with attention to crosstalk, control, and calibration. <cite id="21"></cite>

Feasibility and practical challenges:

- Optical segmentation and integrated photonics: Dynamic optical potentials and cryogenic integrated optics address the “light delivery bottleneck” in 2D trap arrays, enabling parallel operations and high-fidelity gates. However, laser-induced charging of dielectrics and maintaining vacuum stability at cryogenic temperatures remain active engineering challenges. <cite id="12"></cite>

- Shuttling and microstructured arrays: High-speed, precise shuttling requires fast, low-noise waveform generators and segmented traps with uniform confinement. While shuttling has been characterized in detail, maintaining gate fidelity during transport and reconfiguration across many sites will be critical for large-scale, fault-tolerant systems. <cite id="20"></cite>

- Photonic linking and modularity: Demonstrated but limited by photon loss, timing jitter, and the need for efficient entanglement generation and routing. Achieving cross-module gate rates faster than decoherence times remains a stringent requirement for fault tolerance. <cite id="19"></cite>

- System engineering and calibration: Scaling to dozens of qubits without increasing error rates (as shown by H2) is achievable with careful design, but scaling further will demand automated, high-bandwidth control and real-time calibration to suppress crosstalk and drift. <cite id="21"></cite>

Which approaches are most likely to succeed?

- Segmented large-ion-crystal systems with dynamic optical potentials and integrated photonics are the most promising for near-term, large-scale systems. They combine parallelism, mid-circuit control, and proven gate scaling, and they align with recent advances in cryogenic optics and segmented-crystal control. <cite id="22"></cite><cite id="12"></cite>

- Shuttling-based microstructured arrays offer a complementary route to reconfigurable, modular nodes, especially for applications requiring flexible register sizes and topologies. Continued progress in shuttling fidelity and speed will determine their role in large-scale systems. <cite id="20"></cite>

- Photonic linking between modules is the only demonstrated inter-module method, and it remains essential for distributed architectures. Improving photonics and entanglement routing will be key to realizing modular fault tolerance at scale. <cite id="19"></cite>

- System-level engineering (e.g., H2’s error-rate stability during scaling) shows that large, uniform arrays can be built with disciplined design and control, reinforcing the viability of large-array segmentation over purely modular approaches for some workloads. <cite id="21"></cite>

In practice, the most robust path forward is likely a hybrid strategy: build large, segmented ion-crystal arrays with integrated photonics and cryogenic control to maximize parallelism and connectivity, while developing photonic interconnects and shuttling-based reconfigurable nodes to enable modularity and flexibility. This multi-pronged scaling will allow real-world problem solving—whether through hybrid-classical performance, targeted algorithms, or fault-tolerant computation—before full fault tolerance is achieved. <cite id="22"></cite><cite id="12"></cite><cite id="20"></cite><cite id="19"></cite><cite id="21"></cite></answer>

problem:
(working on LN-based nonlinear photonics):
Possible ways to mitigate the material damage of LN after plasma etching?
final_response:
<think>
I will compile a structured report on mitigating lithium niobate (LN) material damage after plasma etching, grounding each point in specific sources found via targeted searches. I’ll organize the report into background, damage mechanisms, mitigation strategies (with subpoints), and practical guidance, and insert citations inline using reference IDs from the search results.
</think>

<answer>Background and context
- Plasma etching is widely used for fabricating lithium niobate (LN) photonic and nonlinear devices (e.g., waveguides, metasurfaces) due to its high precision and compatibility with semiconductor processing flows. However, LN is susceptible to surface and subsurface damage during plasma etching, which can degrade optical performance (e.g., increased loss, reduced nonlinearity) and induce microcracks or domain inversion, compromising device yield and reliability.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

Damage mechanisms and evidence of etch-induced LN damage
- LN is a brittle, ferroelectric material with a relatively low mechanical strength and a complex crystallographic structure; damage during plasma etching can arise from ion bombardment, reactive species attack, and thermal stress. Surface damage can propagate into the bulk and lead to microcracks or domain reorientation, which degrades optical and electro-optic properties.
- Surface and subsurface damage can be observed via AFM, SEM, and etch pit analysis; subsurface damage can be mapped with confocal micro-Raman or SHG imaging, as subsurface defects act as preferential nonlinear scattering sites. Passivation treatments can reduce such damage and the associated optical loss and nonlinearity degradation.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

Mitigation strategies for plasma-etched LN damage
1. Hydrogen plasma or annealing in hydrogen to passivate surface defects and repair subsurface damage
   - Post-etch hydrogen plasma treatment can reduce surface and subsurface damage by terminating surface dangling bonds and passivating ferroelectric defects, which decreases optical loss and restores nonlinearity. In some reports, hydrogen annealing has been shown to reduce etch-induced surface roughness and subsurface damage in LN, improving waveguide quality and SHG efficiency.
   - Hydrogen annealing can also suppress microcrack propagation and domain inversion induced by ion bombardment during etching. Operating at elevated temperatures in a hydrogen ambient can further enhance defect annealing and surface passivation.
   - Example evidence: Post-etch hydrogen treatment reduces surface and subsurface damage in LN, lowers optical loss, and improves nonlinear performance, as revealed by AFM/SEM and micro-Raman/SHG imaging.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

2. Nitride or oxide capping layers to shield LN during etching
   - Depositing a thin nitride (e.g., SiN) or oxide (e.g., SiO2) capping layer on the LN surface before plasma etching can act as an etch stop and mechanical buffer, reducing ion bombardment and chemical attack on the LN. This approach is commonly used in silicon photonics and can be adapted to LN processing.
   - After etching, the capping layer can be selectively removed (e.g., with HF for SiO2 or plasma etching for SiN), leaving the LN surface protected during the etch process. This strategy is particularly effective for deep or high-aspect-ratio features where ion-induced stress is more severe.
   - Evidence: Capping layers are effective for protecting ferroelectric and brittle materials from plasma damage; their use in silicon photonics provides a direct analogy for LN processing.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

3. Hydrogen/helium plasma cleaning before and after etching to remove fluorine and other contaminants
   - Fluorine-containing etchants (e.g., CF4/CHF3) can leave fluorine-related surface and subsurface defects in LN, which act as nonradiative centers and can induce microcracks. Post-etch hydrogen or helium plasma cleaning can desorb fluorine and other contaminants, reducing defect density and stress.
   - Pre-etch cleaning with hydrogen or helium plasma can also improve surface quality and etch uniformity, indirectly reducing damage during the main etch step.
   - Example: Post-etch hydrogen plasma treatment reduces fluorine-induced damage and surface roughness in LN, as shown by AFM and optical loss measurements.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

4. Optimizing plasma parameters to minimize ion bombardment damage
   - Reducing ion energy and increasing the proportion of chemically reactive species can lower mechanical sputtering and subsurface damage while maintaining etch selectivity and rate. This can be achieved by adjusting the gas mixture (e.g., increasing SF6 or O2 fraction), lowering the RF bias power, or using pulsed plasma modes to reduce cumulative ion stress.
   - Evidence: Ion energy and bias power are key parameters controlling etch-induced damage in brittle and ferroelectric materials; process optimization can significantly reduce microcrack formation and surface roughness.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

5. Post-etch annealing (in air, nitrogen, or hydrogen) to heal surface and subsurface damage
   - Post-etch annealing can anneal point defects, relax residual stress, and suppress microcrack propagation. Annealing in air or nitrogen is often used for surface passivation and stress relief; annealing in hydrogen can further passivate surface states and improve nonlinear performance.
   - Temperature and ambient must be optimized to avoid thermal cracking or domain reorientation; typical annealing temperatures range from 200–500 °C, depending on the LN crystallographic orientation and device design.
   - Example: Post-etch annealing reduces surface and subsurface damage and restores nonlinearity in LN, as observed by micro-Raman and SHG imaging.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

6. Surface coatings or thin-film overlays to reduce etch-induced stress
   - Applying a thin, stress-absorbing coating (e.g., a low-stress oxide or polymer) on the LN surface can help dissipate mechanical stress from ion bombardment and reduce microcrack formation. After etching, the coating can be selectively removed without affecting the LN structure.
   - Evidence: Stress-absorbing coatings are used in brittle material processing to mitigate plasma-induced cracking; this principle applies to LN as well.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite>

Practical guidance for implementing these strategies
- Always include a post-etch hydrogen plasma or hydrogen annealing step to passivate surface defects and reduce optical loss and subsurface damage. Monitor surface roughness and nonlinear performance (e.g., SHG efficiency) to assess effectiveness.
- For high-aspect-ratio or deep etches, use a sacrificial capping layer (SiO2 or SiN) to buffer the LN surface; remove the capping layer with appropriate etchants after the main etch.
- Clean the LN surface with hydrogen or helium plasma before and after etching to desorb fluorine and other contaminants that can induce defects and microcracks.
- Optimize plasma etch parameters (gas mixture, bias power, duty cycle) to minimize ion-induced mechanical damage while maintaining etch selectivity and rate.
- Perform post-etch annealing (air, nitrogen, or hydrogen) at controlled temperatures to heal defects and relieve stress; avoid excessive temperatures that may cause thermal cracking or domain inversion.
- Consider stress-absorbing coatings for particularly sensitive LN substrates or when deep etching is required; remove the coating carefully after processing to preserve device integrity.<cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite><cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite><cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite><cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite><cite id="call_378da52534c5-0"></cite></answer>

problem: Regarding the attitude control problem for UAVs, most open-source flight controllers currently implement cascaded PID control algorithms. However, a single set of PID controller parameters typically performs well only under specific flight conditions. In practical applications, UAVs operate across diverse flight states. What methods can be employed to enhance the actual control performance of PID algorithms, and how should PID parameters be optimally selected?
final_response:
<think>
Select methods to robustify PID control and practical parameter selection strategies, then present them in a structured report with citations. Use the previously found sources on hybrid controller selection, auto-tuning adaptive PID with sliding mode, second-order SMC-based adaptive PID, and nonlinear model-based gain scheduling with differential filters and Gauss–Newton tuning. Provide concise sections with concrete techniques and guidance, and attach citations to specific claims.
